title: Aircraft Ultrasonic Inspection | UT for Aerospace (US)
description: Ultrasonic NDT of aircraft parts, forgings, GSE and tooling for US aerospace manufacturers, suppliers and MROs, to your spec. Request a UT inspection quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing for Aviation and Aerospace Parts in the US
html:
Atlantis NDT provides on-site ultrasonic testing for aerospace manufacturers, suppliers, tooling shops and maintenance operations in the United States. That includes aircraft ultrasonic inspection of metallic components and structure when the customer's specification calls for it: forgings, plate and bar stock, machined fittings, structural welds, ground support equipment and fixtures, and thickness checks on corroded metal. Technicians travel to your site and work to your specification and flow-down. To start, request a UT inspection quote with the part list and governing document.

What ultrasonic NDT on aircraft parts actually covers

People searching for ultrasonic NDT of aircraft often mean one of two jobs. The first is examining the metal that goes into an aircraft before it is machined and installed: billet, bar, plate and forgings in aluminum, titanium and high-strength steel. Internal discontinuities such as inclusions, laminations, porosity and forging laps cannot be seen from outside, and contact or immersion ultrasonics is the established way to find them. The second is examining metallic structure or hardware that is already in service or in repair, where the question is cracking at a fastener hole or corrosion thinning of a skin or fitting.

Atlantis supports both kinds of work for customers who have the authority to specify them. We apply the customer's procedure, calibration blocks and acceptance criteria, and report indications against that document. Composite structure and bond-line work require techniques outside this offer, so this page covers metallic parts only.

Who decides airworthiness, and who does not

Maintenance, preventive maintenance and alterations on US-registered aircraft are governed by 14 CFR Part 43, and certificated repair stations operate under 14 CFR Part 145. Those repair stations, and the people they authorize, sign off the work and return the aircraft to service. Atlantis does not sign off airworthiness or return aircraft to service. When our technician examines a part for a repair station or manufacturer, the result is data supplied to the customer, whose quality system decides disposition. FAA Advisory Circular 43.13-1B gives acceptable methods for aircraft inspection and repair, and the customer's own manuals and OEM instructions remain the controlling documents.

Specifications and flow-down

Aerospace UT is normally driven by a customer or prime specification rather than by a general code. A purchase order may invoke an AMS material or process specification such as AMS 2630 for ultrasonic inspection of product over half an inch thick, an ASTM practice such as ASTM E2375 for wrought products or ASTM E114 for contact pulse-echo, and the customer's own process control document with its acceptance classes. Reference standards come from ASTM E127 for aluminum blocks, or from the customer's approved reference set. Those documents set the entry surface finish, scan overlap, sensitivity and recording requirements.

Our personnel are qualified under the company written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A and aligned to the customer's flow-down requirements. A Level II technician performs and interprets; an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies, so a customer that requires additional qualification steps should state them at quoting time, and we will tell you plainly whether they fit.

Wrought stock, forgings and machined parts

Most manufacturing UT is performed on simple geometry, because a flat or round shape gives clean sound entry. Plate and bar are scanned in straight-beam mode against a flat-bottom-hole or comparable reference block, with sensitivity set according to the specification's class. Forgings are harder: the part shape changes the sound path, so a procedure must define scan directions, surface conditions and areas of reduced coverage. After machining, the part may have fillets and thin ribs that cannot be scanned; a good procedure names those areas as not covered and the customer decides how to treat them.

Where the examination takes place affects the technique. Immersion systems are common in a supplier plant; contact scanning is used when the part is large, heavy or fixed, and a mobilized technician commonly works with the contact method on the floor of the customer's shop. We use the equipment your procedure allows and list the instrument, probe and couplant in the report. Couplants for aerospace work are chosen to be removable and compatible with the material; the customer's specification may restrict the type.

Ground support equipment, tooling and fixtures

Not every airport and plant steel structure is an aircraft part. Ground support equipment, such as stands, jacks, lifting beams, towing arms and docking platforms, carries people and aircraft loads, and its welds crack in service. Tooling and assembly fixtures also support heavy aerostructure during build. A crack in a fixture can shift an assembly by a measurable amount before anyone sees it. UT is useful for thickness checks on corroded members and for examining the volume of thick welds; the surface methods, magnetic particle inspection and liquid penetrant testing, handle surface cracks in the same equipment. The owner's engineer decides load rating and repair; our work provides the data.

Corrosion and thickness work

Thickness gauging is the other half of aerospace UT. The method follows ASME Section V, Article 5, in principle, and ASTM E797 for manual contact practice, though aerospace customers frequently supply their own work instruction. Corrosion on fittings, lugs and structural members can reduce wall below the drawing minimum. Thin sheet and skin are difficult for conventional gauges, since the signal needs enough thickness to separate echoes. The procedure fixes the probe and the minimum thickness the setup can measure, and any reading below that is reported as not measurable instead of guessed.

Sensitivity, reference blocks and why they matter

An aerospace ultrasonic examination is only as meaningful as its reference. The specification defines a sensitivity level, often expressed as the response from a flat-bottom hole of a stated diameter at a stated depth, or as a distance-amplitude curve built from several such holes. The technician sets the instrument on a block made of the same alloy and similar thickness as the part, applies any transfer correction for surface finish or curvature, and checks the setting often. A drifting gain or a worn probe can hide a real indication, which is why the checks are written into the report and not left to memory.

Titanium and some nickel alloys scatter sound because of coarse or banded microstructure, which raises the background noise and can bury a small flaw. Aluminum plate has a more favorable grain but can have directional properties. A procedure written for one alloy form cannot be assumed to apply to another, so the Level III reviews the procedure against the actual material before a mobilized job begins.

Planning around plant and maintenance schedules

Aerospace sites run on controlled processes, and an outside examiner has to fit into them. Expect to supply a visitor or contractor badge process, a safety orientation, and in some plants an export-control briefing before our technicians enter. Parts may be quarantined until the report is released, so the date the report is needed is part of the scope. Tell us which parts are on a hold, which are in process and which are returns, and we will plan the order of work accordingly. Instruments, couplants and any consumables are listed at quoting, along with what the plant wants to supply from its own stores.

Technique points that show up in the report

  • Calibration: reference blocks match the part's alloy and acoustic properties, and calibration is checked at start, at intervals and at the end of each examination.
  • Surface condition: machined or ground surfaces suit scanning; as-forged or painted surfaces may need preparation, and the report records what was done.
  • Coverage: scan paths and overlap are recorded, and areas that cannot be scanned from accessible surfaces are listed.
  • Recording: indications are recorded with position, depth, amplitude against reference and the evaluation class, with a sketch.
  • Traceability: part number, serial or lot, drawing revision and heat number are kept so the report ties to the part it covers.

What the report contains

The UT report identifies the customer, part number, serial or lot, drawing revision, material and heat. It lists the governing specification and revision, the acceptance class, the written procedure number, the instrument, probe, couplant and reference blocks, the calibration check results and the scan plan. Indications are listed with location, depth, size or amplitude and the accept or reject decision against the stated limit, with a sketch. The technician and level and the ASNT Level III reviewer are named. Anything not examined, and the reason, is stated.

What to send for a quote

  • The part list with part numbers, materials, dimensions and quantities
  • The specification, flow-down clause and acceptance class, with the revision
  • Whether you need contact or immersion work, and the equipment your site provides
  • Site location, security or ITAR access requirements and safety orientation
  • Any qualification steps your quality system requires of the examiner

Where we work in the US aerospace market

We mobilize to plants and maintenance sites in these aerospace regions.

  • Wichita: business-jet and airframe manufacturing and the supplier network around it.
  • Seattle: Puget Sound airframe, structures and machining suppliers.
  • Hartford: engine, landing gear and precision component manufacturing in Connecticut.
  • Charleston: aerostructure assembly and its supply chain.
  • Savannah: large business aircraft production and support.
  • Fort Worth: military aircraft, helicopters and suppliers in north Texas.
  • Oklahoma City: air logistics and maintenance depot work.
  • Huntsville: missile, launch and space-hardware fabrication.

Training your own technicians

If your plant builds its own UT team, our UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training follow ASNT SNT-TC-1A, and the ultrasonic simulator gives practice before hands-on time. We also write employer procedures through written practice development aligned to a customer flow-down. See aviation NDT training for the industry programs and the national UT page for the method overall.

What we do not do here

Atlantis is not a radiography provider in the United States. We do not examine composites or bonded structure, we do not offer specialist techniques on this page, and we do not sign off airworthiness. Where a customer specification requires a qualification or approval that Atlantis does not hold, we will say so before work is scheduled.

faq.q: Can you perform aircraft ultrasonic inspection on site?
faq.a: We examine metallic parts and structure to a customer's specification at the customer's site, such as forgings, fittings, plate and thickness checks. We provide data to the customer, whose certificated repair station or quality system decides on disposition.

faq.q: Do you sign off airworthiness after an ultrasonic inspection?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not sign off airworthiness or return aircraft to service. Under 14 CFR Parts 43 and 145 that authority belongs to certificated persons and repair stations, and our report is an input to their decision.

faq.q: What does ultrasonic NDT on aircraft components look for?
faq.a: Internal discontinuities in wrought stock and forgings, such as inclusions, laminations and porosity, plus cracking in metallic parts where the geometry allows scanning, and corrosion thinning measured by thickness gauging.

The one on your purchase order or in your work instruction. It might be an AMS specification, an ASTM practice such as E2375, or a customer process document, and we apply its sensitivity, coverage and acceptance class.

faq.q: Can UT be used on aluminum and titanium parts?
faq.a: Yes. Both are examined routinely, using reference blocks of matching alloy. Titanium often needs a tailored procedure because of grain structure, and thin aluminum sheet may be below what a gauge can measure.

They are qualified under the Atlantis written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A and aligned to your flow-down. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies. Tell us at quoting if your quality system adds steps for the examiner.

faq.q: What do you need to quote UT on aerospace parts?
faq.a: Part numbers, material, sizes and quantities, the specification and acceptance class with revision, the equipment available, site location and any security or export-control access rules.

faq.q: Is ultrasonic testing better than penetrant or magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: They find different flaws. UT looks inside the material, while MT and PT find surface cracks. Many aerospace parts need both a volume and a surface method, depending on the specification.

faq.q: Do you inspect ground support equipment?
faq.a: Yes. We examine welds and thickness on stands, jacks, lifting beams and similar equipment, and pair UT with the surface methods. Load rating and repair decisions stay with the equipment owner's engineer.
